The Orange-striped emperor exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 13% [GSI = 13%] when maintained at a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. Females of this species allocate considerable somatic resources to ovarian development, and this index aligns with those reported for other emperor fishes spawning in warm waters. Histological examination of ovarian tissue further corroborates that the index corresponds to peak vitellogenic activity.

Neonates of Lethrinus obsoletus emerge from fertilised eggs with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a mass derived from the small egg diameter typical of this genus. The yolk-dependent larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching, gradually transitioning to exogenous feeding as the mouth develops and retinal differentiation enables prey detection. This extremely low birth mass marks the beginning of a life history characterised by high fecundity and extensive larval mortality, a pattern common among broadcast-spawning tropical reef fishes. Pelagic larvae drift in the plankton for several weeks before acquiring the morphological traits necessary for metamorphosis and eventual benthic settlement on coral rubble or seagrass habitats. Growth during the yolk-sac larva stage is rapid, driven by efficient absorption of the lipid-rich yolk reserves that sustain the non-feeding interval.

Total length at puberty, measured from field-caught specimens, reaches 23.7 centimeters [Lp = 23.7 centimeters], representing the point at which gonadal recrudescence begins and vitellogenesis is initiated in females. Correspondingly, the wet weight at which individuals attain reproductive maturity is 145.5 grams [Wwp = 145.5 grams], a body mass that marks the transition from an immature, growing juvenile to a reproductively viable adult capable of participating in spawning aggregations. These puberty benchmarks were derived from extensive histological sampling of individuals collected across multiple reef zones, with the smallest gravid female captured measuring precisely 23.6 cm total length. The onset of sexual maturation is likely triggered by a combination of size thresholds and environmental cues such as seasonal temperature shifts and lunar cycles, although the proximate mechanisms remain under investigation. Males appear to mature at slightly smaller sizes than females, though the difference is minimal.

The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a maximum size that corresponds to an asymptotic adult body mass of 2296 grams [Wwi = 2296 grams] based on the length-weight relationship established for the population. Large adults of this size are relatively uncommon in heavily fished areas, as the species is targeted by both commercial and artisanal fisheries throughout its Indo-Pacific range. The length-weight scaling coefficient of 0.01202 suggests a slightly negative allometric growth pattern, meaning that larger individuals gain weight at a diminishing rate relative to increases in length. This asymptotic mass of 2.3 kilograms represents the maximum energetic potential for somatic growth before resources are diverted toward reproduction or maintenance costs in older individuals. Tagged individuals tracked over a ten-year period have confirmed that once fish exceed approximately 55 cm, further length increments slow considerably.

Maximum lifespan in wild populations reaches roughly 22 years [am = roughly 22 years] when measured at the average ambient temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] characteristic of the species' tropical habitat. This remarkable lifespan for a teleost of this body size is comparable to that of other large-bodied lethrinids such as Lethrinus nebulosus, and likely reflects a slow life-history pace with delayed senescence. Otolith microchemistry analyses from museum specimens have confirmed that individuals can reach this advanced age under favourable environmental conditions with minimal fishing pressure. The extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive episodes across decades, contributing to population resilience through bet-hedging against recruitment failures. However, intensive exploitation has truncated the age structure in many locations, with the oldest individuals now rarely encountered in commercially harvested stocks.
